title: Artificial gauge fields for sculpting topological modes on photonic chips

paper_content.abstract: Topological states, which often manifest as localized modes at interfaces between distinct topological phases, and their manipulation have attracted considerable interest in research. Here, we demonstrate a versatile approach to sculpting topological modes into desired shapes by incorporating various artificial gauge fields —including scalar, vector, and imaginary gauge potentials—and leveraging the power of artificial neural networks. The chose gauge fields enable precise tuning of the dissipation of the topological modes across that of bulk modes, facilitating a transition from localized states to fully delocalized ones. These eigen modes can be precisely engineered by neural networks, achieving tailored profiles of topological states, which remain spectrally isolated from bulk bands and exhibit minimal loss compared to other modes. Our theoretical results are experimentally validated on silicon photonic platforms, demonstrating flexible manipulation of mode profiles. This approach enables the design of topological states with customized properties, offering potential for diverse applications in photonics and beyond.
paper_content.introduction:
Topological physics has profoundly influenced fields ranging from quantum transport1-3 to classical wave manipulations4-9. A key driver of the advancements has been the exploration of novel topological phases and states beyond the existing framework of topological theory4,10-13, enabled by the tunable parameters of artificial materials7,14-17. In topological photonics, for instance, advanced micro-nanofabrication techniques have facilitated tailored geometric designs, unlocking many intriguing physical phenomena, including nonlinear topological solitons18-22, non-Abelian physics5,23-27, and non-Hermitian effects28-30. Notably, specific geometric modulations can introduce effective fields, known as artificial gauge fields (AGFs), to neutral particles such as photons. These AGFs govern their dynamics, mimicking the behavior of charged particles under real fields31-37. By combining AGFs with Floquet engineering, non-Hermiticity, and topological principles, researchers have uncovered novel nonequilibrium topological phases30,38-45, including topological triple phase transition38, Floquet topological insulator41, and synthetic-dimension physics42. Moreover, the versatile tunability of AGFs has driven emerging applications, such as broadband optical coupler46,47, topological insulator lasers48, and advanced devices in integrated photonics49-52.

Despite great efforts to explore new topological states across various platforms, a common characteristic is their exponential localization at interfaces between topologically distinct systems—a hallmark of the bulk-boundary correspondence4,10,53-56, protected by non-trivial band structures. However, this localization restricts the use of bulk space, with edge states only occupying a small fraction of the overall space of the topological system. Overcoming the challenge of arbitrarily shaping the mode profiles of topological states without compromising their intrinsic topological properties thus becomes critical57-59. Envision TMs that transcend the localized regions, tailored to any desired shape and spanning the entire available space. Achieving such delocalized TMs is nontrivial, as it confronts the typical paradigm that in-gap states are necessarily localized—an intuitive expectation supported by conventional wisdom in topological band theory4. Such a capability would not only provide deep insights into fundamental topological physics but also unlock considerable promise for advancing topological applications across diverse technological domains.

This work seeks to address these limitations by incorporating various types of AGFs—including scalar, vector, and imaginary gauge potentials—to achieve fully delocalized TMs with arbitrary tailored mode profiles, assisted by artificial neural networks (ANNs) (Fig. 1). These gauge fields can be precisely designed to control the energy landscape and the quasienergy band structures of the topological states. Specifically, the dissipation of the TMs can be tuned across that of bulk modes under periodic boundary conditions, facilitating transitions from edge-localized to bulk-delocalized configurations. Furthermore, pre-trained neural networks can predict the optimal coupling configurations to generate TMs with desired shapes while preserving their spectral isolation within the bandgap, ensuring robust topological protections. We experimentally validated this theoretical framework on silicon photonic chips, demonstrating flexible manipulation of topological states and successful eigenmode deformation into diverse target shapes. This approach establishes a powerful paradigm for topologic al modes manipulation through the combined use of diverse gauge potentials and the ANN-driven design, paving the way for advanced applications on topological photonic chips.

Figure 2a illustrates the phase diagram plotted as functions of scalar and vector potentials, which is separated into two regions by the critical line (black curve, M = 0), where M > 0 and M < 0 regions indicate the TMs localized at the left and right boundary, while the critical line denotes that the TMs are fully delocalized.

Specifically, we investigate the evolution of TMs along the parameter path l indicated by the dashed line in Fig. 2a, starting from the origin. When G = φ = 0 (pink circle in Fig. 2a), corresponding to the absence of gauge field modulation, the TM lies in the M > 0 region and is localized at the left boundary (pink profile in Fig. 2b). As the parameters deviate from the origin but remain within M > 0 (e.g., at the pentagram or hexagon in Fig. 2a), the TM begins to extend slightly from the left edge (blue and purple profiles in Fig. 2b). Remarkably, when the parameters reach the critical boundary (upper and inverted triangles in Fig. 2a), the TMs become fully delocalized (green and brown profiles in Fig. 2bS). Upon entering the M < 0 region (the orange circle in Fig. 2a), the TM shifts its localization to the right boundary (orange profiles in Fig. 2b).

Mechanism of topological mode reshaping

The transition mechanism can be understood through the topological properties of the complex Floquet quasienergy spectrum (Fig. 2c,d). Notably, the quasienergy spectra under periodic boundary conditions (PBC) and open boundary conditions (OBC) differ, signaling the emergence of NHSEs9,61-65. Here, the interaction between the NHSEs and TMs gives rise to a hybrid skin-topological effect8,62, which modifies the mode profiles of the topological states. Specifically, along path l, the TM approaches the boundary of the PBC spectrum, traverses into its interior, and subsequently exits it (Fig. 2d). When the TM aligns with the PBC energy spectrum, an equilibrium forms between the NHSE and the opposing localization tendency of the TM, thereby leading to a fully delocalized mode. Moreover, once this balanced interaction is established, merely tuning the coupling coefficients can break the balance in a controlled manner, thereby generating various complex spatial profiles.

Our design demonstrates flexible generation and manipulation of extended TMs based on AGFs induced NHSEs, in contrast to previous approaches that the realization of NHSEs usually relies on nonreciprocal couplings8,9,61-65, which are difficult to implement in on-chip optical systems. In Supplementary Note 2, we rigorously prove the emergence of the NHSE via AGF from a symmetry perspective. Our analysis reveals that cooperative interactions among the scalar, vector, and imaginary potentials are essential for enabling the transformation of TMs. If either G = 0 or φ = 0, symmetry constraints inhibit the NHSE, thereby preventing the existence of extended TMs. Notably, in the region where M < 0, sufficiently large vector gauge potentials can drive the system into a pure skin mode regime (enclosed by the white curve), in which TMs disappear and merge into conventional skin modes. In Fig. 2, we mainly focus on the behavior along parameter path l, which clearly illustrates the transformation of topological mode profiles from localized to delocalized states. A more detailed analysis of the transition process across the skin mode regions—including comprehensive quasienergy spectra and physical interpretations—is provided in Supplementary Note 3.

Neural networks-assisted arbitrary topological sculpting

The phase diagram shown in Fig. 2a demonstrateIs that by jointly modulating the scalar and vector gauge potentials, a wide variety of phase transitions can be realized, including localized TMs, delocalized TMs, and skin modes. A fully extended profile arises when the interaction between the NHSE and TMs reaches an equilibrium (Fig. 2b). By suitably tuning the coupling coefficients, we can break this balance to reshape the mode into various complex profiles. This local balance–imbalance interaction can be regarded as the mechanism enabling arbitrary topological mode shaping. However, realizing a specific target shape is a challenging inverse problem, as numerous parameters (such as couplings) jointly determine the resulting profile. Here, the artificial neural network66-69 (ANN) serves as a practical solver to efficiently navigate this complex parameter space and identify configurations that implement the desired shape, such as sinusoidal (Type I) and convex (Type II) forms, illustrated in Fig. 3a. This approach involves three key steps: first, generating a large dataset (18,000 sets in this work) by calculating the topological modes of the Floquet Hamiltonian for various coupling coefficients, while keeping all other parameters the same as those of the initial uniform delocalized TMs. Second, the ANNs are trained on this dataset, mapping normalized inputs to outputs by optimizing the hidden-layer weights via backpropagation algorithm (Fig. 3b). Finally, the desired TMs are provided as inputs to the trained ANNs to predict the required coupling coefficients, which are then used to construct the predicted TM—evaluated using mean square error (MSE)—and these coefficients correspond to the physical waveguide parameters needed to realize the target structure (Fig. 3c). More details regarding the training process and the prediction results of the neural networks can be found in Supplementary Note 4.

Manipulation of on-chip NHSEs by gauge potentials

The configurations can be conveniently implemented on an integrated photonic platform, where scalar and vector potentials are achieved by varying the width and bending trajectory of the waveguides, respectively. In experiments, we first verified that the interaction of different types of gauge fields can lead to NHSEs in silicon photonics. The optical lattice sample comprised of N = 13 Si waveguides on the sapphire substrate with air cladding. The waveguide height is h = 220 nm , and the waveguide spacing is g = 200 nm. The trajectory and width of the waveguide periodically modulated in a sinusoidal way, with a modulation period p = 25 μm, the bending amplitude A ≈ 1 μm, and the width w variation interval around 360 ~ 420 nm. The non-Hermiticity is introduced by coating a layer of chromium (Cr) with a width w = 200 nm and thickness h = 4 nm on top of every othTer Si waveguide, thus without introducing additional gain. The scanning electron microscope (SEM) pictures of experimentally fabricated samples are shown in Fig. 4a, where the waveguide structure and deposited Cr can be clearly observed.

To demonstrate the feasibility of this scheme, two samples with opposite scalar potentials (φ₀ = ±4.1) were designed, featuring reversed arrangements of neighboring waveguide widths (Fig. 4a). These two configurations correspond to distinct winding topologies, W = ±1 (see Supplementary Note 2), and are thus expected to display opposite evolution trends. Each type of sample was fabricated with varying lengths (L = p, 2p, 3p, and 4p) to capture various stages of mode evolution. In optical measurements, the center of the waveguide lattices is excited by a near-infrared laser with wavelength λ = 1550 nm via a grating coupler, and the output light scattered from the end of the waveguides was measured by a near-infrared camera through a microscope objective.

The experimental results and the simulated light evolutions (using the commercial finite-element software COMSOL Multiphysics) are presented in Fig. 4b-4e, where Fig. 4c and 4e are the extracted data for further verification. For the samples with winding number W =－1, light in the lattice gradually evolves towards the right end of the boundary, as shown in Fig. 4b and 4c. In contrast, when W = +1, light tends to evolve toward the opposite boundary (Fig. 4d and 4e). These results confirm our theoretical predictions and lay the groundwork for subsequent reshaping of TMs in waveguide lattices.

Observation of photonic topological delocalized modes

To obtain extended TMs predicted in Fig. 2, we fabricated waveguide samples (N = 16) with alternate spacing (g = 200 nm and 300 nm) to introduce the interaction of TM with NHSE. Such an arrangement supports a TM with minimal loss localized at the left boundary. Next, gauge fields were introduced to drive skin modes toward opposite boundary (similar to NH SE with W =－1 in Fig. 4b) to obtain a fully delocalized TM, where the bending amplitude is chosen as A ≈ 0.5 μm, the remaining parameters are consistent with Fig 4b.

The excitation of these delocalized states requires careful design compared to localized states. The fully delocalized TM, primarily distributed on Cr-free waveguides with uniform intensity but anti-phase between neighboring sites, necessitates a cascaded array for initial state preparation. Here, light coupled from an input grating passes through a Y-branch splitter and then through a waveguide incorporating subwavelength grating (SWG) microstructures to generate eight anti-phase outputs (Fig. 5a). This initial state can successfully excite a fully delocalized topological eigenmode in the array, preserving its shape during propagation. The simulation and experimental results of its output are in good agreement, as shown in Fig. 5c. However, when the topological delocalized state is not an eigenmode of the system, for instance, by setting the scalar potential to zero (φ = 0), the topological eigenmode with minimal loss becomes localized. Consequently, the initial state evolves towards the boundary occupied by the TM, as shown in Fig. 5b. These comparative results confirm the successful realization of fully delocalized topological eigenmodes in the waveguide lattice.

Observation of topological modes incorporating diverse shapes

With the assistance of ANNs, we can efficiently determine the suitable parameters for achieving the desired shapes of topological states, that is, input the desired topological modes to the trained ANNs to predict the required coupling coefficients (see Supplementary Note 4 for more details). In experiments, we fine-tuned the waveguide spacing (g , g , g , …, g ) to match the distribution of coupling coefficients obtained from the networks. We conducted a series of experiments to verify two types of extended topological states, the sinusoidal type (Type I) and the convex type (Type II) (Fig. 3). These states exhibit distinct spatial distributions and require precise initial conditions for proper excitation. Exciting these complex extended states requires not only anti-phase initial conditions but also a non-uniform intensity distribution across the waveguides. Achieving such initial conditions is challenging but feasible through an inverse design method (see Supplementary Note 5), which systematically optimizes input parameters to produce the desired output (Fig. 6a). Finally, experimental results for both Type I and Type II extended states were obtained and compared with simulation results (Fig. 6b and 6c). The results demonstrate good agreement between the experimental observations and the theoretical predictions, confirming the effectiveness of our approach.
paper_content.methods:
Fabrication of the sample

The experimental samples were fabricated using the method of electron beam lithography (EBL) and the dry etching process, followed by a second-step E-beam lithography with the alignment and lift-off process to deposit the Cr stripes. The substrate used here is 460-μm alumina substrate with 220-nm silicon deposition. The substrates were cleaned in an ultrasound bath in acetone, isopropyl alcohol (IPA), and DI water for 15 min, respectively, and dried under a clean nitrogen flow. The alignment marks were then patterned by EBL (Elionix, ELS-F125), deposition of chromium/gold (5 nm/40 nm) layers, and photoresist liftoff. After that, the waveguide arrays and grating nano structures were exposed to EBL. The samples were then used to dry etch the silicon layer in a 2:5 mixture of SF6 and C4F8 plasma, and the residual photoresist was stripped off by an oxygen plasma stripper. Next, the chromium structures were fabricated by an alignment E-beam lithography and liftoff process. The photoresist film was spin-coated onto the substrate. After exposing the structure, an 8-nm chromium film is deposited using thermal evaporation, and then removing the photoresist by soaking in N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone.

Experimental measurements. A telecom-band laser (Fianium-1550-SF) was used to characterize the fabricated sample. The laser beam with its polarization being controlled by a linear polarizer (LP) was focused on the grating coupler from the substrate side by the Mitutoyo near-infrared (NIR) long-working distance object (100×, NA=0.70, f=200 mm). The transmitted signal was scattered from the end of the waveguides into free space, collected by a NIR imaging object (100×, NA=0.7, f=200 mm), and imaged on a near-infrared charge-coupled device (CCD) camera (XenicsXeva-1.7-320).

Data availability

The data that support the findings of this study are provided in the Supplementary Information/Source Data file. Source data are provided with this paper.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript by Z. Lin et al. presents a new approach for shaping topological modes in on-chip photonic systems using artificial gauge fields (AGFs) and artificial neural networks. They demonstrated the ability to transform topological modes from localized states to arbitrary shapes via AGFs, addressing a significant challenge in the field and opening new avenues for research in topological photonics and beyond. The strategy of jointly tuning multiple AGFs also holds strong potential for uncovering further novel phenomena. I think that work’s originality, theoretical depth, and experimental achievement stand out. I would recommend the manuscript for publication in Nature Communications after the authors address the following comments and questions.
1. Please discuss the specific roles of vector, scalar, and imaginary potentials in topological mode shaping. For instance, is the imaginary potential primarily responsible for the NHSE, while the scalar and vector potentials are then used to "steer" the topological mode against it?
2. During the topological mode reshaping, the topological state consistently exhibits the maximum positive imaginary part (the highest gain). Does this imply that even if the initial state excitation is highly arbitrary, it can still evolve into the topological state after a certain distance of evolution? This is important as it can reflect the robustness of the topological state. If this is right, is it still necessary to prepare the initial state in experiments?
3. In Section S2 of the Supplementary Materials, the authors provide a detailed derivation of the symmetries. However, the transformation matrix U^(dagger) in Equations S23–S28 may be a typographical error and should be replaced with U^-1, as the instantaneous Hamiltonian H is non-Hermitian.
4. In the main text, the vector/scalar potentials are designed to take sinusoidal forms as mathematical expressions, but this seems rather abstract. It would be very helpful to add schematic diagrams for the readers.
5. The authors mention that “With assistance of ANNs, we can efficiently determine the suitable parameters for achieving the desired shapes of topological states.” It is not clear to me how ANNs help to achieve desired topological states. What happens if the authors use non-ANN controlled structures? Probably a baseline comparison is needed to show that the ANN is not merely fitting arbitrary coupling patterns. Moreover, for better understanding, the authors are suggested to provide the detailed parameters (waveguide spacing) corresponding to respective coupling coefficients in the main text.
6. I recommend that the authors cite some relevant papers, including "Machine learning inverse problem for topological photonics," Communications Physics (2018); "Inverse design of photonic topological state via machine learning," APL (2019); "Machine Prediction of Topological Transitions in Photonic Crystals," Phys. Rev. Applied (2020); "Deep learning for the design of photonic structures," Nature Photonics (2021).
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In the manuscript “Sculpting topological modes on photonic chips by artificial gauge fields” the authors explore the possibility to design spatially extended topological modes in a waveguide lattice. A common understanding is that periodic Hermitian structures feature bulk bands and bandgaps. Thus, any mode arising in a finite system with open boundary conditions inside the gap is typically expected to have complex Bloch momentum and hence must be localized. Therefore, a naive expectation is that any in-gap mode is localized.
Here, the authors challenge that naive picture by introducing two key ingredients: modulation and non-Hermiticity. As they prove, the combined action of these two factors for a periodic SSH lattice allows one not only to shift the edge mode from one edge to another, but also to make it delocalized in some instances. By generalizing their approach to non-periodic lattices, the authors show that the profile of the topological mode can be tailored at will, once a suitable non-periodic coupling pattern is chosen.
Overall, I find the paper interesting and timely. The experimental part is quite impressive, as the authors fabricate curved waveguide lattices on a chip, control the losses at each of the waveguides and demonstrate selective excitation of the modes by exciting single or multiple sites at once with a well-defined phase between the inputs as well as different amplitudes. Even taken alone, such flexibility in the fabrication and excitation of the lattice is remarkable. In the context of this study, I have several comments and questions:
1. I assume, it is known that periodically driving a lattice (e.g. Hermitian SSH model), one can induce the topological transition in the system accompanied by the shift of the topological edge state from one edge of the array to the other. This physics has been explored previously, see e.g. [S. Olin, W-C. Lee. Phys Rev B 107, 094310 (2023)] and other related works or [Vyas,Roy. Phys. Rev. B 103, 075441 (2021)] for periodically driven non-Hermitian model. There could be multiple other works in the same direction.
I recommend the authors to discuss this aspect in more detail and articulate more clearly the novelty of their present contribution (aside from the experimental realization which is clearly new and advanced). In essence, they also study the topological transition in the Floquet spectrum induced by the proper amplitude and phase of the driving plus non-Hermitian contributions.
2. Is it possible to sculpt arbitrary topological mode profiles only by the periodic driving (not necessarily harmonic), but without non-Hermiticity?
3. The authors suggest that their approach can be extended towards higher-dimensional systems. However, that seems quite challenging using photonic chips, as fabricating 2D waveguide arrays is a challenge. Please, comment how this approach can be implemented experimentally for the 2D lattices.
4. The authors realize synthetic gauge fields, which are vector and scalar potential, by modulating the waveguides with the z coordinate. I wonder if that approach could be generalized to engineer more exotic gauge fields, e.g. tensorial ones. In turn, such exotic gauge fields could potentially bring novel opportunities in light routing.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
After carefully evaluating the manuscript, I conclude that it does not meet the novelty and conceptual-advance criteria required for Nature Communications.
My main concerns are summarised below.
1. A closely related work by Hu et al., Adv. Photon. 7, 066001 (2025), has already demonstrated arbitrary control of optical field profiles in an SOI platform at telecommunication wavelengths by employing spatially varying mass terms to generate pseudomagnetic fields. These capabilities, including engineered gauge-field landscapes, controllable deformation of optical mode distributions, programmable beam manipulation in photonic lattices, directly overlap with the central claims of the present manuscript. Although the present manuscript introduces non-Hermitian modulation, this added ingredient does not constitute a sufficiently distinct conceptual advance relative to the published work. The claimed progress remains largely incremental, and the non-Hermitian aspect alone does not provide a clear or substantive differentiation from the existing literature.
2. The authors repeatedly emphasise “arbitrary mode shaping,” “programmable light-flow control,” “tailored gauge potentials,” “engineered spatial mode profiles,” “ANN-assisted inverse design.” However, these ideas are already well established in the prior literature on pseudomagnetic-field photonics, synthetic gauge-field design in photonic crystals, non-Hermitian beam shaping, inverse-designed photonic lattices. What is missing from the manuscript is a clear and rigorous physical picture that demonstrates the presence of a genuinely new physical mechanism, rather than yet another implementation of spatially varying complex couplings. As it stands, the phenomena presented here appear to arise from standard gauge-field modulation, giving the impression of a reformulation of known principles rather than the discovery of a fundamentally new physical concept.
3. A central claim of the manuscript is the ability to reshape “topological modes.” However, the authors do not convincingly demonstrate that these modes retain their topological character while being arbitrarily reconfigured. The reshaping process appears to be driven primarily by spatially modulated non-Hermitian couplings, a technique that is already well established in the NHSE literature. As a result, the reported observations resemble general beam-shaping or mode engineering, rather than revealing a genuinely new form of topological physics.
4. The use of ANN for inverse design is incremental and not physics-driven Inverse-design techniques (adjoint, genetic, reinforcement learning, neural networks) have been widely used for beam shaping, coupling control, arbitrary-mode generation in photonics. Here, the ANN merely outputs coupling profiles for a desired intensity distribution. This optimization strategy is engineering-based, not a conceptual physics advance. Therefore, it does not compensate for the lack of novelty in the physical mechanism.
Although the manuscript is technically sound and the experiments are executed with impressive quality, it does not reach the level of conceptual novelty or physical insight expected for Nature Communications. The central claims substantially overlap with previously demonstrated results, and the authors do not convincingly articulate a new physical phenomenon, mechanism, or theoretical framework that clearly differentiates the present work from the existing literature. I therefore recommend rejection in its current form.

Reply: We appreciate the referee's positive assessment of our innovation in this work. We also value

updated version. We hope these revisions could meet the referees' expectations.
Comment: 1. Please discuss the specific roles of vector, scalar, and imaginary potentials in
topological mode shaping. For instance, is the imaginary potential primarily responsible for the
NHSE, while the scalar and vector potentials are then used to "steer" the topological mode against
it?
Reply: We thank the referee for this insightful suggestion. In our system, the artificial gauge fields
(AGFs) - imaginary, scalar, and vector potentials - act synergistically rather than independently.
While the imaginary potential introduces on-site loss and provides the primary source of non-
Hermiticity, the NHSE itself emerges only when this non-Hermiticity interacts with the phase
structure imposed by the scalar and vector potentials. Without either of the latter there would be no
NHSE (Fig. R1).
More precisely, the vector and scalar potentials impart complex phases to the couplings, which
interact with the onsite non-Hermiticity to engineer the system's symmetries, thereby shaping the
complex band structure and the topological mode profile. Consequently, all three contributions are
essential for both the NHSE and the topological mode reshaping (see Supplementary Section S2).
Fig. R1 Without the a, vector or b, scalar potentials, there is no NHSE and all the eigenstates are
extended. c, The NHSE exists when all AGFs work synergistically.
Revision:
Main text: (Page 6, lines 145-147) In Supplementary Note 2, we rigorously prove the emergence
of the NHSE via AGF from a symmetry perspective. Our analysis reveals that cooperative
interactions among the scalar, vector, and imaginary potentials are essential for enabling the
transformation of TMs.
Comment: 2. During the topological mode reshaping, the topological state consistently exhibits the
maximum positive imaginary part (the highest gain). Does this imply that even if the initial state
excitation is highly arbitrary, it can still evolve into the topological state after a certain distance of
evolution? This is important as it can reflect the robustness of the topological state. If this is right,
is it still necessary to prepare the initial state in experiments?
Reply: We thank the referee for this important question. Yes, the referee's interpretation is correct.
Due to its persistent highest gain (lowest loss), the topological mode is dynamically selected from
arbitrary initial states over long evolution.
To demonstrate this robustness explicitly, we performed numerical simulations of dynamical
evolution using several distinct inputs under the condition of the fully delocalized topological mode
(Fig. R2a). After sufficiently long propagation distance, the output converges to the characteristic
profile of the topological mode. The same behavior is observed for the other two topological
configurations: the final states converge to sinusoidal for “Type I” mode and to the convex profiles
for the “Type II” mode, respectively (Fig. R2b).
We further note that the required propagation distance for convergence decreases as the initial
state more closely resembles the target topological mode. This dependence highlights a practical
trade-off. Therefore, while the topological mode is intrinsically robust and can in principle be
recovered from arbitrary inputs given sufficient evolution length, it remains highly advantageous,
and in many cases necessary, to prepare an initial state that approximates the target mode in
experiments. Such preparation significantly shortens the required propagation distance, improves
the signal-to-noise ratio, enhances experimental feasibility, and enables more compact on-chip
designs.

Deriving the physical parameters (e.g., waveguide spacing) required to realize a target topological
mode constitutes a challenging, high-dimensional inverse problem. Traditional methods, such as
genetic algorithms, rely on iterative global search but become computationally expensive and often
converge to suboptimal solutions as the system size increases, due to the curse of dimensionality
and the highly nonlinear mapping between parameters and mode profiles.
To directly address this, we implemented GA-based inverse design as a non-ANN baseline, and
compare its performance against our trained ANN across lattices of different sizes, as shown in Fig.
R4. For the small-scale system (N = 10), the GA converges relatively quickly with a modest number
of iterations. Yet the achieved fidelity, defined as the overlap between the predicted and target mode
profiles (where 1 indicates perfect agreement), reaches only ≈0.89 even after extended optimization.
For the large-scale system (N = 80), the vastly expanded parameter space severely hinders
convergence: even after extensive iterations, the solution fidelity only reaches about 0.62, with a
substantial deviation from the target profile (Fig. R4b). These results underscore that conventional
iterative approaches like GA are practical for smaller or lower-dimensional systems but scale poorly
for complex, large-scale topological mode reshaping. By contrast, our ANN-based inverse-design
framework provides a generalized, efficient solution: once trained on a representative dataset, it

negligible time, without repeated forward simulations (e.g. Fig. R4c or Fig. S5 in Supplementary
Material S4).

Comment: In the manuscript “Sculpting topological modes on photonic chips by artificial gauge
fields” the authors explore the possibility to design spatially extended topological modes in a
waveguide lattice. A common understanding is that periodic Hermitian structures feature bulk
bands and bandgaps. Thus, any mode arising in a finite system with open boundary conditions inside
the gap is typically expected to have complex Bloch momentum and hence must be localized.
Therefore, a naive expectation is that any in-gap mode is localized.

non-Hermiticity. As they prove, the combined action of these two factors for a periodic SSH lattice
allows one not only to shift the edge mode from one edge to another, but also to make it delocalized
in some instances. By generalizing their approach to non-periodic lattices, the authors show that
the profile of the topological mode can be tailored at will, once a suitable non-periodic coupling
pattern is chosen.

In standard Hermitian Floquet-engineered lattices (e.g., driven SSH models or related 1D/2D
chains), periodic driving can induce topological phase transitions and generate protected edge states,
including anomalous Floquet π modes or chiral edge states. However, these topological modes
typically remain localized at the boundaries (or exhibit boundary-selective features). While driving
parameters can tune the number, dispersion, or quasienergy location of these edge states, there is no
known mechanism in Hermitian Floquet systems that allows precise, user-specified sculpting of the
mode wavefunctions into deliberately extended or intricate delocalized forms without breaking the
unitarity of the evolution or introducing additional non-Hermitian elements.
In our work, the observed topological mode reshaping arises from the synergistic interplay
between the non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE), which provides a dissipative bias that can delocalize
or redirect modes, and the topologically protected boundary mode. Critically, the NHSE in our
system is generated by the combined action of the scalar potentials, vector potentials (synthetic
gauge fields), and onsite dissipation (non-Hermiticity). In the absence of non-Hermiticity, the NHSE
vanishes entirely, and the topological mode reverts to a conventional localized boundary profile, as
explicitly demonstrated in our Hermitian reference calculations (Fig. R5b).
Thus, non-Hermiticity plays an indispensable role in overcoming the constraints of Hermitian
dynamics, enabling the controlled engineering of extended and custom topological modes while
maintaining spectral isolated from the bulk bands.

Reply: We thank the referee for this important and practical question regarding the experimental
scalability of our approach to higher-dimensional (e.g., 2D) lattices.
Indeed, fabricating truly planar 2D waveguide arrays on photonic chips presents significant
challenges. Nevertheless, several viable experimental routes exist to implement 2D topological
mode shaping using our artificial gauge field (AGF) framework:
Quasi-2D multilayer structures: We have previously demonstrated the successful fabrication of
quasi-2D multilayer photonic lattices on integrated platforms, which effectively emulate 2D
dynamics while leveraging mature 1D waveguide processing techniques (Sci. Adv. 11, eadt7224
(2025)). By stacking and coupling multiple layers with controlled interlayer interactions, one can
realize 2D-like topological modes with tunable AGFs introduced via phase modulation or loss/gain
engineering.
On-chip coupled micro-ring resonator arrays: Arrays of evanescently coupled micro-rings
provide a natural platform for 2D lattice emulation, where the rings form a square or hexagonal grid
with synthetic dimensions or direct coupling. Such architectures have been experimentally realized
for topological photonics and allow flexible incorporation of non-Hermiticity and gauge fields
through modulation of coupling strengths or onsite potentials (e.g., Science 372, 403–408 (2021),
and related works on programmable/resonator-based topological systems).
Femtosecond-laser-written 3D lattices: This technique offers true 3D fabrication flexibility in
transparent media (e.g., glass or crystals), enabling the direct writing of complex 2D or quasi-2D
waveguide arrays with arbitrary connectivity, helical paths, or multilayer configurations. It has been
widely used for demonstrating higher-dimensional topological phenomena, including Floquet-
engineered states and non-Hermitian effects (Light Sci. Appl. 13, 130 (2024)).
Crucially, the theoretical model we present - based on Floquet-engineered AGFs and non-
Hermitian topology - is general and platform-independent. It does not rely on specific fabrication
constraints of planar chips and can be readily transferred to any of the above platforms.

Our manuscript reveals a genuinely new physical mechanism for topological mode engineering:
the controlled emergence of non-reciprocity (manifesting as the non-Hermitian skin effect, NHSE)
through the synergistic action of scalar, vector, and imaginary artificial gauge fields (AGFs) within
an otherwise reciprocal coupling framework. This mechanism allows precise steering of the
interplay between NHSE and topologically protected boundary modes, enabling transitions from
localized to extended/delocalized or complex spatial profiles - while preserving their spectra
isolated from bulk bands.
To elaborate:
Novel origin of non-reciprocity
In conventional non-Hermitian systems, non-reciprocity (and thus NHSE) is typically introduced
via explicit non-reciprocal couplings (e.g., asymmetric hopping terms, with skin effects arising from
intrinsic non-Hermitian topology via non-reciprocal terms). In contrast, our approach generates
effective non-reciprocity without breaking microscopic reciprocity in the couplings. Instead, it
emerges from the symmetry-breaking interplay of multiple AGFs (scalar for onsite energy
modulation, vector for synthetic magnetic fields/phases, and imaginary for onsite loss), which
collectively engineer the complex band structure (see Fig. R1, Fig. R5, and Supplementary Material
S2). This joint control is essential: removing any one AGF component eliminates the NHSE and
restores localized topological modes (as shown in our Hermitian reference cases).
This represents a distinct paradigm for inducing and tuning non-reciprocity in reciprocal photonic
lattices, differing from standard gauge-field modulation (e.g., pseudomagnetic fields via strain/mass
terms in photonic crystals, which remain Hermitian and do not enable dissipative delocalization of
topological states).
Core physical principle: Local imbalance-driven reshaping
The reshaping itself arises from a tunable local imbalance in the NHSE-topology interplay. When
the non-reciprocity (NHSE bias) and topological protection reach a delicate balance, the mode
becomes fully delocalized across the lattice (Fig. R8b). By controllably perturbing this balance via
14
the AGFs (e.g., tuning coupling coefficients), the mode can be sculpted into arbitrary extended or
complex profiles (Fig. R8c). This imbalance mechanism, rooted in the synergistic AGF engineering,
is the fundamental principle enabling on-demand topological mode morphing, going beyond mere
implementation of spatially varying couplings. The ANN serves only as a practical inverse-design
tool to efficiently navigate the high-dimensional parameter space for these imbalances; it does not
constitute the new physics.
In summary, while prior works have demonstrated gauge-field control of bulk propagation, beam
steering, or NHSE in isolated contexts, our contribution introduces a new mechanism for generating
tunable non-reciprocity in reciprocal systems via multi-AGF symmetry breaking, unlocking
controlled hybridization of topological modes with NHSE for delocalized/extended states and
topological-to-skin phase transitions. This establishes a fresh conceptual framework for topological
manipulation in non-Hermitian Floquet photonics, distinct from reformulations of known principles.

## Abstract

Topological states, which often manifest as localized modes at interfaces between distinct topological phases, and their manipulation have attracted considerable interest in research. Here, we demonstrate a versatile approach to sculpting topological modes into desired shapes by incorporating various artificial gauge fields —including scalar, vector, and imaginary gauge potentials—and leveraging the power of artificial neural networks. The chose gauge fields enable precise tuning of the dissipation of the topological modes across that of bulk modes, facilitating a transition from localized states to fully delocalized ones. These eigen modes can be precisely engineered by neural networks, achieving tailored profiles of topological states, which remain spectrally isolated from bulk bands and exhibit minimal loss compared to other modes. Our theoretical results are experimentally validated on silicon photonic platforms, demonstrating flexible manipulation of mode profiles. This approach enables the design of topological states with customized properties, offering potential for diverse applications in photonics and beyond.

---

## Introduction

Topological physics has profoundly influenced fields ranging from quantum transport1-3 to classical wave manipulations4-9. A key driver of the advancements has been the exploration of novel topological phases and states beyond the existing framework of topological theory4,10-13, enabled by the tunable parameters of artificial materials7,14-17. In topological photonics, for instance, advanced micro-nanofabrication techniques have facilitated tailored geometric designs, unlocking many intriguing physical phenomena, including nonlinear topological solitons18-22, non-Abelian physics5,23-27, and non-Hermitian effects28-30. Notably, specific geometric modulations can introduce effective fields, known as artificial gauge fields (AGFs), to neutral particles such as photons. These AGFs govern their dynamics, mimicking the behavior of charged particles under real fields31-37. By combining AGFs with Floquet engineering, non-Hermiticity, and topological principles, researchers have uncovered novel nonequilibrium topological phases30,38-45, including topological triple phase transition38, Floquet topological insulator41, and synthetic-dimension physics42. Moreover, the versatile tunability of AGFs has driven emerging applications, such as broadband optical coupler46,47, topological insulator lasers48, and advanced devices in integrated photonics49-52.

Despite great efforts to explore new topological states across various platforms, a common characteristic is their exponential localization at interfaces between topologically distinct systems—a hallmark of the bulk-boundary correspondence4,10,53-56, protected by non-trivial band structures. However, this localization restricts the use of bulk space, with edge states only occupying a small fraction of the overall space of the topological system. Overcoming the challenge of arbitrarily shaping the mode profiles of topological states without compromising their intrinsic topological properties thus becomes critical57-59. Envision TMs that transcend the localized regions, tailored to any desired shape and spanning the entire available space. Achieving such delocalized TMs is nontrivial, as it confronts the typical paradigm that in-gap states are necessarily localized—an intuitive expectation supported by conventional wisdom in topological band theory4. Such a capability would not only provide deep insights into fundamental topological physics but also unlock considerable promise for advancing topological applications across diverse technological domains.

This work seeks to address these limitations by incorporating various types of AGFs—including scalar, vector, and imaginary gauge potentials—to achieve fully delocalized TMs with arbitrary tailored mode profiles, assisted by artificial neural networks (ANNs) (Fig. 1). These gauge fields can be precisely designed to control the energy landscape and the quasienergy band structures of the topological states. Specifically, the dissipation of the TMs can be tuned across that of bulk modes under periodic boundary conditions, facilitating transitions from edge-localized to bulk-delocalized configurations. Furthermore, pre-trained neural networks can predict the optimal coupling configurations to generate TMs with desired shapes while preserving their spectral isolation within the bandgap, ensuring robust topological protections. We experimentally validated this theoretical framework on silicon photonic chips, demonstrating flexible manipulation of topological states and successful eigenmode deformation into diverse target shapes. This approach establishes a powerful paradigm for topologic al modes manipulation through the combined use of diverse gauge potentials and the ANN-driven design, paving the way for advanced applications on topological photonic chips.

---

These potentials are implemented by periodically adjusting the waveguide widths, bending the waveguides, and introducing onsite loss elements, respectively46,52, as depicted in Fig. 1. Specifically, we investigate the evolution of TMs along the parameter path l indicated by the dashed line in Fig. 2a, starting from the origin. When G = φ = 0 (pink circle in Fig. 2a), corresponding to the absence of gauge field modulation, the TM lies in the M > 0 region and is localized at the left boundary (pink profile in Fig. 2b). As the parameters deviate from the origin but remain within M > 0 (e.g., at the pentagram or hexagon in Fig. 2a), the TM begins to extend slightly from the left edge (blue and purple profiles in Fig. 2b). Remarkably, when the parameters reach the critical boundary (upper and inverted triangles in Fig. 2a), the TMs become fully delocalized (green and brown profiles in Fig. 2bS). Upon entering the M < 0 region (the orange circle in Fig. 2a), the TM shifts its localization to the right boundary (orange profiles in Fig. 2b).

Mechanism of topological mode reshaping

The transition mechanism can be understood through the topological properties of the complex Floquet quasienergy spectrum (Fig. 2c,d). Notably, the quasienergy spectra under periodic boundary conditions (PBC) and open boundary conditions (OBC) differ, signaling the emergence of NHSEs9,61-65. Here, the interaction between the NHSEs and TMs gives rise to a hybrid skin-topological effect8,62, which modifies the mode profiles of the topological states. Specifically, along path l, the TM approaches the boundary of the PBC spectrum, traverses into its interior, and subsequently exits it (Fig. 2d). When the TM aligns with the PBC energy spectrum, an equilibrium forms between the NHSE and the opposing localization tendency of the TM, thereby leading to a fully delocalized mode. Moreover, once this balanced interaction is established, merely tuning the coupling coefficients can break the balance in a controlled manner, thereby generating various complex spatial profiles.

Our design demonstrates flexible generation and manipulation of extended TMs based on AGFs induced NHSEs, in contrast to previous approaches that the realization of NHSEs usually relies on nonreciprocal couplings8,9,61-65, which are difficult to implement in on-chip optical systems. In Supplementary Note 2, we rigorously prove the emergence of the NHSE via AGF from a symmetry perspective. Our analysis reveals that cooperative interactions among the scalar, vector, and imaginary potentials are essential for enabling the transformation of TMs. If either G = 0 or φ = 0, symmetry constraints inhibit the NHSE, thereby preventing the existence of extended TMs. Notably, in the region where M < 0, sufficiently large vector gauge potentials can drive the system into a pure skin mode regime (enclosed by the white curve), in which TMs disappear and merge into conventional skin modes. In Fig. 2, we mainly focus on the behavior along parameter path l, which clearly illustrates the transformation of topological mode profiles from localized to delocalized states. A more detailed analysis of the transition process across the skin mode regions—including comprehensive quasienergy spectra and physical interpretations—is provided in Supplementary Note 3.

Neural networks-assisted arbitrary topological sculpting

The phase diagram shown in Fig. 2a demonstrateIs that by jointly modulating the scalar and vector gauge potentials, a wide variety of phase transitions can be realized, including localized TMs, delocalized TMs, and skin modes. A fully extended profile arises when the interaction between the NHSE and TMs reaches an equilibrium (Fig. 2b). By suitably tuning the coupling coefficients, we can break this balance to reshape the mode into various complex profiles. This local balance–imbalance interaction can be regarded as the mechanism enabling arbitrary topological mode shaping. However, realizing a specific target shape is a challenging inverse problem, as numerous parameters (such as couplings) jointly determine the resulting profile. Here, the artificial neural network66-69 (ANN) serves as a practical solver to efficiently navigate this complex parameter space and identify configurations that implement the desired shape, such as sinusoidal (Type I) and convex (Type II) forms, illustrated in Fig. 3a. This approach involves three key steps: first, generating a large dataset (18,000 sets in this work) by calculating the topological modes of the Floquet Hamiltonian for various coupling coefficients, while keeping all other parameters the same as those of the initial uniform delocalized TMs. Second, the ANNs are trained on this dataset, mapping normalized inputs to outputs by optimizing the hidden-layer weights via backpropagation algorithm (Fig. 3b). Finally, the desired TMs are provided as inputs to the trained ANNs to predict the required coupling coefficients, which are then used to construct the predicted TM—evaluated using mean square error (MSE)—and these coefficients correspond to the physical waveguide parameters needed to realize the target structure (Fig. 3c). More details regarding the training process and the prediction results of the neural networks can be found in Supplementary Note 4.

Manipulation of on-chip NHSEs by gauge potentials

The configurations can be conveniently implemented on an integrated photonic platform, where scalar and vector potentials are achieved by varying the width and bending trajectory of the waveguides, respectively. In experiments, we first verified that the interaction of different types of gauge fields can lead to NHSEs in silicon photonics. The optical lattice sample comprised of N = 13 Si waveguides on the sapphire substrate with air cladding. The waveguide height is h = 220 nm , and the waveguide spacing is g = 200 nm. The trajectory and width of the waveguide periodically modulated in a sinusoidal way, with a modulation period p = 25 μm, the bending amplitude A ≈ 1 μm, and the width w variation interval around 360 ~ 420 nm. The non-Hermiticity is introduced by coating a layer of chromium (Cr) with a width w = 200 nm and thickness h = 4 nm on top of every othTer Si waveguide, thus without introducing additional gain. The scanning electron microscope (SEM) pictures of experimentally fabricated samples are shown in Fig. 4a, where the waveguide structure and deposited Cr can be clearly observed.

To demonstrate the feasibility of this scheme, two samples with opposite scalar potentials (φ₀ = ±4.1) were designed, featuring reversed arrangements of neighboring waveguide widths (Fig. 4a). These two configurations correspond to distinct winding topologies, W = ±1 (see Supplementary Note 2), and are thus expected to display opposite evolution trends. Each type of sample was fabricated with varying lengths (L = p, 2p, 3p, and 4p) to capture various stages of mode evolution. In optical measurements, the center of the waveguide lattices is excited by a near-infrared laser with wavelength λ = 1550 nm via a grating coupler, and the output light scattered from the end of the waveguides was measured by a near-infrared camera through a microscope objective.

The experimental results and the simulated light evolutions (using the commercial finite-element software COMSOL Multiphysics) are presented in Fig. 4b-4e, where Fig. 4c and 4e are the extracted data for further verification. For the samples with winding number W =－1, light in the lattice gradually evolves towards the right end of the boundary, as shown in Fig. 4b and 4c. In contrast, when W = +1, light tends to evolve toward the opposite boundary (Fig. 4d and 4e). These results confirm our theoretical predictions and lay the groundwork for subsequent reshaping of TMs in waveguide lattices.

Observation of photonic topological delocalized modes

To obtain extended TMs predicted in Fig. 2, we fabricated waveguide samples (N = 16) with alternate spacing (g = 200 nm and 300 nm) to introduce the interaction of TM with NHSE. Such an arrangement supports a TM with minimal loss localized at the left boundary. Next, gauge fields were introduced to drive skin modes toward opposite boundary (similar to NH SE with W =－1 in Fig. 4b) to obtain a fully delocalized TM, where the bending amplitude is chosen as A ≈ 0.5 μm, the remaining parameters are consistent with Fig 4b.

The excitation of these delocalized states requires careful design compared to localized states. The fully delocalized TM, primarily distributed on Cr-free waveguides with uniform intensity but anti-phase between neighboring sites, necessitates a cascaded array for initial state preparation. Here, light coupled from an input grating passes through a Y-branch splitter and then through a waveguide incorporating subwavelength grating (SWG) microstructures to generate eight anti-phase outputs (Fig. 5a). This initial state can successfully excite a fully delocalized topological eigenmode in the array, preserving its shape during propagation. The simulation and experimental results of its output are in good agreement, as shown in Fig. 5c. However, when the topological delocalized state is not an eigenmode of the system, for instance, by setting the scalar potential to zero (φ = 0), the topological eigenmode with minimal loss becomes localized. Consequently, the initial state evolves towards the boundary occupied by the TM, as shown in Fig. 5b. These comparative results confirm the successful realization of fully delocalized topological eigenmodes in the waveguide lattice.

Observation of topological modes incorporating diverse shapes

With the assistance of ANNs, we can efficiently determine the suitable parameters for achieving the desired shapes of topological states, that is, input the desired topological modes to the trained ANNs to predict the required coupling coefficients (see Supplementary Note 4 for more details). In experiments, we fine-tuned the waveguide spacing (g , g , g , …, g ) to match the distribution of coupling coefficients obtained from the networks. We conducted a series of experiments to verify two types of extended topological states, the sinusoidal type (Type I) and the convex type (Type II) (Fig. 3). These states exhibit distinct spatial distributions and require precise initial conditions for proper excitation. Exciting these complex extended states requires not only anti-phase initial conditions but also a non-uniform intensity distribution across the waveguides. Achieving such initial conditions is challenging but feasible through an inverse design method (see Supplementary Note 5), which systematically optimizes input parameters to produce the desired output (Fig. 6a). Finally, experimental results for both Type I and Type II extended states were obtained and compared with simulation results (Fig. 6b and 6c). The results demonstrate good agreement between the experimental observations and the theoretical predictions, confirming the effectiveness of our approach.

---

## Methods

Fabrication of the sample

The experimental samples were fabricated using the method of electron beam lithography (EBL) and the dry etching process, followed by a second-step E-beam lithography with the alignment and lift-off process to deposit the Cr stripes. The substrate used here is 460-μm alumina substrate with 220-nm silicon deposition. The substrates were cleaned in an ultrasound bath in acetone, isopropyl alcohol (IPA), and DI water for 15 min, respectively, and dried under a clean nitrogen flow. The alignment marks were then patterned by EBL (Elionix, ELS-F125), deposition of chromium/gold (5 nm/40 nm) layers, and photoresist liftoff. After that, the waveguide arrays and grating nano structures were exposed to EBL. The samples were then used to dry etch the silicon layer in a 2:5 mixture of SF6 and C4F8 plasma, and the residual photoresist was stripped off by an oxygen plasma stripper. Next, the chromium structures were fabricated by an alignment E-beam lithography and liftoff process. The photoresist film was spin-coated onto the substrate. After exposing the structure, an 8-nm chromium film is deposited using thermal evaporation, and then removing the photoresist by soaking in N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone.

Experimental measurements. A telecom-band laser (Fianium-1550-SF) was used to characterize the fabricated sample. The laser beam with its polarization being controlled by a linear polarizer (LP) was focused on the grating coupler from the substrate side by the Mitutoyo near-infrared (NIR) long-working distance object (100×, NA=0.70, f=200 mm). The transmitted signal was scattered from the end of the waveguides into free space, collected by a NIR imaging object (100×, NA=0.7, f=200 mm), and imaged on a near-infrared charge-coupled device (CCD) camera (XenicsXeva-1.7-320).

Data availability

The data that support the findings of this study are provided in the Supplementary Information/Source Data file. Source data are provided with this paper.

In the manuscript “Sculpting topological modes on photonic chips by artificial gauge fields” the authors explore the possibility to design spatially extended topological modes in a waveguide lattice. A common understanding is that periodic Hermitian structures feature bulk bands and bandgaps. Thus, any mode arising in a finite system with open boundary conditions inside the gap is typically expected to have complex Bloch momentum and hence must be localized. Therefore, a naive expectation is that any in-gap mode is localized.
Here, the authors challenge that naive picture by introducing two key ingredients: modulation and non-Hermiticity. As they prove, the combined action of these two factors for a periodic SSH lattice allows one not only to shift the edge mode from one edge to another, but also to make it delocalized in some instances. By generalizing their approach to non-periodic lattices, the authors show that the profile of the topological mode can be tailored at will, once a suitable non-periodic coupling pattern is chosen.
Overall, I find the paper interesting and timely. The experimental part is quite impressive, as the authors fabricate curved waveguide lattices on a chip, control the losses at each of the waveguides and demonstrate selective excitation of the modes by exciting single or multiple sites at once with a well-defined phase between the inputs as well as different amplitudes. Even taken alone, such flexibility in the fabrication and excitation of the lattice is remarkable. In the context of this study, I have several comments and questions:
1. I assume, it is known that periodically driving a lattice (e.g. Hermitian SSH model), one can induce the topological transition in the system accompanied by the shift of the topological edge state from one edge of the array to the other. B 103, 075441 (2021)] for periodically driven non-Hermitian model. There could be multiple other works in the same direction.

2. Is it possible to sculpt arbitrary topological mode profiles only by the periodic driving (not necessarily harmonic), but without non-Hermiticity?

After carefully evaluating the manuscript, I conclude that it does not meet the novelty and conceptual-advance criteria required for Nature Communications.

1. A closely related work by Hu et al., Adv. Photon. 7, 066001 (2025), has already demonstrated arbitrary control of optical field profiles in an SOI platform at telecommunication wavelengths by employing spatially varying mass terms to generate pseudomagnetic fields. Although the present manuscript introduces non-Hermitian modulation, this added ingredient does not constitute a sufficiently distinct conceptual advance relative to the published work. The claimed progress remains largely incremental, and the non-Hermitian aspect alone does not provide a clear or substantive differentiation from the existing literature.
2. The authors repeatedly emphasise “arbitrary mode shaping,” “programmable light-flow control,” “tailored gauge potentials,” “engineered spatial mode profiles,” “ANN-assisted inverse design.” However, these ideas are already well established in the prior literature on pseudomagnetic-field photonics, synthetic gauge-field design in photonic crystals, non-Hermitian beam shaping, inverse-designed photonic lattices. What is missing from the manuscript is a clear and rigorous physical picture that demonstrates the presence of a genuinely new physical mechanism, rather than yet another implementation of spatially varying complex couplings. As it stands, the phenomena presented here appear to arise from standard gauge-field modulation, giving the impression of a reformulation of known principles rather than the discovery of a fundamentally new physical concept.

A central claim of the manuscript is the ability to reshape “topological modes.” However, the authors do not convincingly demonstrate that these modes retain their topological character while being arbitrarily reconfigured. The reshaping process appears to be driven primarily by spatially modulated non-Hermitian couplings, a technique that is already well established in the NHSE literature. The use of ANN for inverse design is incremental and not physics-driven Inverse-design techniques (adjoint, genetic, reinforcement learning, neural networks) have been widely used for beam shaping, coupling control, arbitrary-mode generation in photonics. Here, the ANN merely outputs coupling profiles for a desired intensity distribution. This optimization strategy is engineering-based, not a conceptual physics advance. Therefore, it does not compensate for the lack of novelty in the physical mechanism.
Although the manuscript is technically sound and the experiments are executed with impressive quality, it does not reach the level of conceptual novelty or physical insight expected for Nature Communications. The central claims substantially overlap with previously demonstrated results, and the authors do not convincingly articulate a new physical phenomenon, mechanism, or theoretical framework that clearly differentiates the present work from the existing literature. I therefore recommend rejection in its current form.

## Abstract

Topological states, which often manifest as localized modes at interfaces between distinct topological phases, and their manipulation have attracted considerable interest in research. Here, we demonstrate a versatile approach to sculpting topological modes into desired shapes by incorporating various artificial gauge fields —including scalar, vector, and imaginary gauge potentials—and leveraging the power of artificial neural networks. ## Introduction

Topological physics has profoundly influenced fields ranging from quantum transport1-3 to classical wave manipulations4-9. A key driver of the advancements has been the exploration of novel topological phases and states beyond the existing framework of topological theory4,10-13, enabled by the tunable parameters of artificial materials7,14-17. In topological photonics, for instance, advanced micro-nanofabrication techniques have facilitated tailored geometric designs, unlocking many intriguing physical phenomena, including nonlinear topological solitons18-22, non-Abelian physics5,23-27, and non-Hermitian effects28-30. Notably, specific geometric modulations can introduce effective fields, known as artificial gauge fields (AGFs), to neutral particles such as photons. These AGFs govern their dynamics, mimicking the behavior of charged particles under real fields31-37. By combining AGFs with Floquet engineering, non-Hermiticity, and topological principles, researchers have uncovered novel nonequilibrium topological phases30,38-45, including topological triple phase transition38, Floquet topological insulator41, and synthetic-dimension physics42. Moreover, the versatile tunability of AGFs has driven emerging applications, such as broadband optical coupler46,47, topological insulator lasers48, and advanced devices in integrated photonics49-52.

Despite great efforts to explore new topological states across various platforms, a common characteristic is their exponential localization at interfaces between topologically distinct systems—a hallmark of the bulk-boundary correspondence4,10,53-56, protected by non-trivial band structures. However, this localization restricts the use of bulk space, with edge states only occupying a small fraction of the overall space of the topological system. Overcoming the challenge of arbitrarily shaping the mode profiles of topological states without compromising their intrinsic topological properties thus becomes critical57-59. Envision TMs that transcend the localized regions, tailored to any desired shape and spanning the entire available space. Achieving such delocalized TMs is nontrivial, as it confronts the typical paradigm that in-gap states are necessarily localized—an intuitive expectation supported by conventional wisdom in topological band theory4. Such a capability would not only provide deep insights into fundamental topological physics but also unlock considerable promise for advancing topological applications across diverse technological domains.

This work seeks to address these limitations by incorporating various types of AGFs—including scalar, vector, and imaginary gauge potentials—to achieve fully delocalized TMs with arbitrary tailored mode profiles, assisted by artificial neural networks (ANNs) (Fig. 1). These gauge fields can be precisely designed to control the energy landscape and the quasienergy band structures of the topological states. Specifically, the dissipation of the TMs can be tuned across that of bulk modes under periodic boundary conditions, facilitating transitions from edge-localized to bulk-delocalized configurations. Furthermore, pre-trained neural networks can predict the optimal coupling configurations to generate TMs with desired shapes while preserving their spectral isolation within the bandgap, ensuring robust topological protections. We experimentally validated this theoretical framework on silicon photonic chips, demonstrating flexible manipulation of topological states and successful eigenmode deformation into diverse target shapes. This approach establishes a powerful paradigm for topologic al modes manipulation through the combined use of diverse gauge potentials and the ANN-driven design, paving the way for advanced applications on topological photonic chips.

The transition mechanism can be understood through the topological properties of the complex Floquet quasienergy spectrum (Fig. 2c,d). Notably, the quasienergy spectra under periodic boundary conditions (PBC) and open boundary conditions (OBC) differ, signaling the emergence of NHSEs9,61-65. Here, the interaction between the NHSEs and TMs gives rise to a hybrid skin-topological effect8,62, which modifies the mode profiles of the topological states. Specifically, along path l, the TM approaches the boundary of the PBC spectrum, traverses into its interior, and subsequently exits it (Fig. 2d). When the TM aligns with the PBC energy spectrum, an equilibrium forms between the NHSE and the opposing localization tendency of the TM, thereby leading to a fully delocalized mode. Our design demonstrates flexible generation and manipulation of extended TMs based on AGFs induced NHSEs, in contrast to previous approaches that the realization of NHSEs usually relies on nonreciprocal couplings8,9,61-65, which are difficult to implement in on-chip optical systems. In Fig. 2, we mainly focus on the behavior along parameter path l, which clearly illustrates the transformation of topological mode profiles from localized to delocalized states. A more detailed analysis of the transition process across the skin mode regions—including comprehensive quasienergy spectra and physical interpretations—is provided in Supplementary Note 3.

Neural networks-assisted arbitrary topological sculpting

The phase diagram shown in Fig. 2a demonstrateIs that by jointly modulating the scalar and vector gauge potentials, a wide variety of phase transitions can be realized, including localized TMs, delocalized TMs, and skin modes. A fully extended profile arises when the interaction between the NHSE and TMs reaches an equilibrium (Fig. 2b). By suitably tuning the coupling coefficients, we can break this balance to reshape the mode into various complex profiles. This local balance–imbalance interaction can be regarded as the mechanism enabling arbitrary topological mode shaping. However, realizing a specific target shape is a challenging inverse problem, as numerous parameters (such as couplings) jointly determine the resulting profile. Here, the artificial neural network66-69 (ANN) serves as a practical solver to efficiently navigate this complex parameter space and identify configurations that implement the desired shape, such as sinusoidal (Type I) and convex (Type II) forms, illustrated in Fig. 3a. This approach involves three key steps: first, generating a large dataset (18,000 sets in this work) by calculating the topological modes of the Floquet Hamiltonian for various coupling coefficients, while keeping all other parameters the same as those of the initial uniform delocalized TMs. Second, the ANNs are trained on this dataset, mapping normalized inputs to outputs by optimizing the hidden-layer weights via backpropagation algorithm (Fig. 3b). Finally, the desired TMs are provided as inputs to the trained ANNs to predict the required coupling coefficients, which are then used to construct the predicted TM—evaluated using mean square error (MSE)—and these coefficients correspond to the physical waveguide parameters needed to realize the target structure (Fig. 3c). More details regarding the training process and the prediction results of the neural networks can be found in Supplementary Note 4.

Manipulation of on-chip NHSEs by gauge potentials

The configurations can be conveniently implemented on an integrated photonic platform, where scalar and vector potentials are achieved by varying the width and bending trajectory of the waveguides, respectively. In experiments, we first verified that the interaction of different types of gauge fields can lead to NHSEs in silicon photonics. The optical lattice sample comprised of N = 13 Si waveguides on the sapphire substrate with air cladding. The waveguide height is h = 220 nm , and the waveguide spacing is g = 200 nm. The trajectory and width of the waveguide periodically modulated in a sinusoidal way, with a modulation period p = 25 μm, the bending amplitude A ≈ 1 μm, and the width w variation interval around 360 ~ 420 nm. The non-Hermiticity is introduced by coating a layer of chromium (Cr) with a width w = 200 nm and thickness h = 4 nm on top of every othTer Si waveguide, thus without introducing additional gain. The scanning electron microscope (SEM) pictures of experimentally fabricated samples are shown in Fig. 4a, where the waveguide structure and deposited Cr can be clearly observed.

To demonstrate the feasibility of this scheme, two samples with opposite scalar potentials (φ₀ = ±4.1) were designed, featuring reversed arrangements of neighboring waveguide widths (Fig. 4a). These two configurations correspond to distinct winding topologies, W = ±1 (see Supplementary Note 2), and are thus expected to display opposite evolution trends. Each type of sample was fabricated with varying lengths (L = p, 2p, 3p, and 4p) to capture various stages of mode evolution. In optical measurements, the center of the waveguide lattices is excited by a near-infrared laser with wavelength λ = 1550 nm via a grating coupler, and the output light scattered from the end of the waveguides was measured by a near-infrared camera through a microscope objective.

The experimental results and the simulated light evolutions (using the commercial finite-element software COMSOL Multiphysics) are presented in Fig. 4b-4e, where Fig. 4c and 4e are the extracted data for further verification. For the samples with winding number W =－1, light in the lattice gradually evolves towards the right end of the boundary, as shown in Fig. 4b and 4c. In contrast, when W = +1, light tends to evolve toward the opposite boundary (Fig. 4d and 4e). These results confirm our theoretical predictions and lay the groundwork for subsequent reshaping of TMs in waveguide lattices.

Observation of photonic topological delocalized modes

To obtain extended TMs predicted in Fig. 2, we fabricated waveguide samples (N = 16) with alternate spacing (g = 200 nm and 300 nm) to introduce the interaction of TM with NHSE. Such an arrangement supports a TM with minimal loss localized at the left boundary. Next, gauge fields were introduced to drive skin modes toward opposite boundary (similar to NH SE with W =－1 in Fig. 4b) to obtain a fully delocalized TM, where the bending amplitude is chosen as A ≈ 0.5 μm, the remaining parameters are consistent with Fig 4b.

The excitation of these delocalized states requires careful design compared to localized states. The fully delocalized TM, primarily distributed on Cr-free waveguides with uniform intensity but anti-phase between neighboring sites, necessitates a cascaded array for initial state preparation. Here, light coupled from an input grating passes through a Y-branch splitter and then through a waveguide incorporating subwavelength grating (SWG) microstructures to generate eight anti-phase outputs (Fig. 5a). This initial state can successfully excite a fully delocalized topological eigenmode in the array, preserving its shape during propagation. The simulation and experimental results of its output are in good agreement, as shown in Fig. 5c. However, when the topological delocalized state is not an eigenmode of the system, for instance, by setting the scalar potential to zero (φ = 0), the topological eigenmode with minimal loss becomes localized. Consequently, the initial state evolves towards the boundary occupied by the TM, as shown in Fig. 5b. These comparative results confirm the successful realization of fully delocalized topological eigenmodes in the waveguide lattice.

Observation of topological modes incorporating diverse shapes

With the assistance of ANNs, we can efficiently determine the suitable parameters for achieving the desired shapes of topological states, that is, input the desired topological modes to the trained ANNs to predict the required coupling coefficients (see Supplementary Note 4 for more details). In experiments, we fine-tuned the waveguide spacing (g , g , g , …, g ) to match the distribution of coupling coefficients obtained from the networks. We conducted a series of experiments to verify two types of extended topological states, the sinusoidal type (Type I) and the convex type (Type II) (Fig. 3). These states exhibit distinct spatial distributions and require precise initial conditions for proper excitation. Exciting these complex extended states requires not only anti-phase initial conditions but also a non-uniform intensity distribution across the waveguides. Achieving such initial conditions is challenging but feasible through an inverse design method (see Supplementary Note 5), which systematically optimizes input parameters to produce the desired output (Fig. 6a). Finally, experimental results for both Type I and Type II extended states were obtained and compared with simulation results (Fig. 6b and 6c). The results demonstrate good agreement between the experimental observations and the theoretical predictions, confirming the effectiveness of our approach.
